The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Let $\Phi:E\to F$ be a smooth vector bundle map over $\operatorname{id}_M$, and
assume that the fibre rank of $\Phi_p:E_p\to F_p$ is the same integer $k$ for
every $p\in M$. Then $\ker\Phi$ is a smooth vector subbundle of $E$ and
$\operatorname{im}\Phi$ is a smooth vector subbundle of $F$.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth vector bundle with connection $\nabla$. For smooth
vector fields $X,Y$ and a smooth section $s$ of $E$, the **curvature of
$\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)s:=\nabla_X\nabla_Ys-\nabla_Y\nabla_Xs-\nabla_{[X,Y]}s.$$

This uses the same sign convention as the curvature of an affine connection.
The next proposition proves that this operator is tensorial and hence is an
$\operatorname{End}(E)$-valued two-form. At this definition stage no metric,
torsion, or bundle trivialization is assumed.

If $M$ is empty, $E$ has rank zero, or $M$ has dimension zero, the displayed
operator is the unique zero curvature operator. For a rank-one bundle and for
a manifold with boundary the same local formula applies without modification.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

Fix integers $N\geq2$ and $k\geq0$. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with their standard Hermitian inner products. A raw framed ADHM datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$, and $J:V\to W$. Its complex and real moment expressions are

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable when the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, for $m\geq0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$, and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable when no nonzero subspace of $V$ is invariant under both $B_1,B_2$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular when it is both stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$ and its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$. The regular zero-FI real quotient is the orbit set

$$\mathcal A^{\mathrm{reg}}_{k,N}=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable and costable}\}/U(V).$$

Let $S^4=\mathbb H\mathbb P^1$ have the unit round metric and the orientation whose restriction to the stereographic coordinates $z_1=x^0+ix^1$, $z_2=x^2+ix^3$ on $\mathbb R^4=S^4\setminus\{\infty\}$ is $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. For a smooth right principal $U(N)$-bundle $P\to S^4$, let $E=P\times_{U(N)}\mathbb C^N$ be its Hermitian associated vector bundle, let $A$ be a smooth unitary connection, and let $\Phi:E|_{\infty}\to\mathbb C^N$ be a unitary framing. Write $F_A$ for the anti-Hermitian curvature matrix and define

$$q_N(P,A)=-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_{S^4}\operatorname{tr}_N(F_A\wedge F_A).$$

The anti-self-dual equation is $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2=0$. For integer $k\geq0$, the framed ASD sector $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}$ is the set of such framed connections satisfying $F_A^+=0$ and $q_N(P,A)=-k$, modulo smooth unitary gauge transformations whose value at $\infty$ is the identity in the framing. This definition alone does not assert that every sector exists or that $q_N$ is integral; the exact $U(N)$ charge normalization is a separate lemma below.

Identify $\mathbb H^2$ with $\mathbb C^4$ using a fixed right quaternionic structure $j$ with $j^2=-1$. The twistor space is $Z=\mathbb C\mathbb P^3=\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb H^2)$, the projection $\pi:Z\to\mathbb H\mathbb P^1=S^4$ sends a complex line $\ell$ to the quaternionic line $\ell+j\ell$, and the antiholomorphic involution is $\sigma([v])=[jv]$. A real twistor line is a fibre $L_x=\pi^{-1}(x)\cong\mathbb C\mathbb P^1$; $\sigma$ restricts to the antipodal map on each such line. Fix homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$ so $\sigma$ is induced by $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)\mapsto(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$. The finite real line over $z$ has equations $\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2$, $\mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2$; the line at infinity is $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0$. These equations fix the quaternionic identification and its orientation. In the chart $\lambda_1=1,\lambda_2=0$, vertical complex orientation followed by the positive orientation of $(z_1,z_2)$ is the complex orientation of $Z$.


For the spinor convention, use the standard spin structure on $S^4$ and $\operatorname{Spin}(4)\cong SU(2)_+\times SU(2)_-$. Let $S^+,S^-$ be the associated rank-two complex spinor bundles, so $T_{\mathbb C}S^4\cong S^+\otimes S^-$. The twistor fibre at $x$ is $\mathbb P(S_x^+)$, and the complex two-plane associated with $\ell\in\mathbb P(S_x^+)$ is $\ell\otimes S_x^-$. Use the Levi-Civita connection of the round metric for the horizontal distribution of $\pi$; the horizontal $(0,1)$ subspace at $[\ell]\in L_x$ projects to this complex alpha-plane. The displayed orientation is the twistor orientation: the vertical complex orientation followed by the quotient orientation on $S^4$ agrees with the complex orientation on $Z$. It is chosen so the curvature component that vanishes on every such plane is precisely $F^+=(F+*_gF)/2$. In spinor components, $F_{AB}=F_{(AB)}$ denotes the symmetric spinor corresponding to $F^+$ under $\Lambda^2_+T_x^*S^4\otimes\mathbb C\cong\operatorname{Sym}^2(S_x^+)^*$; restriction to the plane is $F_{AB}\pi^A\pi^B$, which vanishes for every $[\pi]\in\mathbb P(S_x^+)$ exactly when $F^+=0$.

A linear monad on $Z$ is a complex of holomorphic bundles

$$\mathcal O_Z(-1)\otimes U\xrightarrow{a}\mathcal O_Z\otimes K\xrightarrow{b}\mathcal O_Z(1)\otimes U',$$

where $U,U',K$ are finite-dimensional complex vector spaces, $b\circ a=0$, $a$ is injective as a sheaf map, $b$ is surjective, and the cohomology sheaf $\ker b/\operatorname{im}a$ is locally free. It is framed when that cohomology has a specified unitary trivialization on $L_\infty$. For a holomorphic bundle $\mathcal E$ on $Z$ that is holomorphically trivial on every real line, a positive Hermitian Ward reality datum is a holomorphic nondegenerate pairing $b:\mathcal E\otimes\sigma^*\overline{\mathcal E}\to\mathcal O_Z$ satisfying $b_{\sigma z}(v,u)=\overline{b_z(u,v)}$. Here $b_z$ is complex linear in $u\in\mathcal E_z$ and conjugate linear in $v\in\mathcal E_{\sigma z}$; the conjugate pullback is holomorphic because $\sigma$ is antiholomorphic. For holomorphic sections $s,t$ on $L_x$, the function $b_z(s(z),t(\sigma z))$ is holomorphic on the compact line, hence constant. It defines $h_x(s,t)$; require this Hermitian form to be positive definite for every $x$. The metric on each fibre of $\mathcal E|_{L_x}$ is transported from this form by holomorphic evaluation. Thus positive forms are induced by the pairing, not independent arbitrary choices. A framed Ward bundle includes a unitary framing on $L_\infty$ for this induced form. Smoothness and parallelness of the induced section-bundle metric are conclusions of the Ward construction.

The compact torus $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$ acts on $\mathbb R^4\cong\mathbb C^2$ by $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(t_1z_1,t_2z_2)$ and on $W$ by $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its raw ADHM action is

$$ (t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ). $$

On the framed ASD sector, the same torus acts by inverse pullback under the indicated rotation of $S^4$ and by postcomposition of the framing with $h$. On $Z$, the rotations act by $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]\mapsto[\lambda_1:t_1t_2\lambda_2:t_1\mu_1:t_2\mu_2]$, equivalently the projective spin lift to $\mathbb P(S^+)$; the central sign in the spin double cover acts trivially after projectivization, and the induced action commutes with $\sigma$. The framing torus acts on the framed monad cohomology by the same diagonal representation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Matrix multiplication gives $b_z^\dagger a_z=(-B_2+z_2)(B_1-z_1)+(B_1-z_1)(B_2-z_2)+IJ=\mu_{\mathbb C}$. Taking adjoints gives the other off-diagonal entry of $DD^\dagger$. Subtracting $a_z^\dagger a_z$ from $b_z^\dagger b_z$ cancels every scalar and linear-in-$z$ term and leaves $[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J=\mu_{\mathbb R}$. This proves both identities with their exact signs.

Failure of surjectivity of $b_z^\dagger=(-B_2+z_2,B_1-z_1,I)$ gives a nonzero covector $\ell$ with $\ell B_i=z_i\ell$ and $\ell I=0$, contradicting the stable spanning set. Conversely, if the stable word span $S$ is proper, the induced pair on $V/S$ commutes since $[B_1,B_2]=-IJ$ has image in $S$. Its dual has a common eigenvector by [F4], and the resulting covector annihilates $I$ and both rows at the corresponding $z$, so surjectivity fails there. A kernel vector of $a_z$ is a common eigenvector of $B_i$ in $\ker J$ and contradicts costability. Conversely, on any nonzero common invariant $S\subset\ker J$, the pair commutes by the complex equation and has a common eigenvector by [F4], producing such a kernel. This proves both equivalences.

Expanding $[A,C]+(I\lambda_1-J^\dagger\lambda_2)(J\lambda_1+I^\dagger\lambda_2)$ gives the stated polynomial with coefficients $\mu_{\mathbb C},\mu_{\mathbb R},-\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger$. Substitution of $\sigma v$ in $\alpha$, followed by adjoint, gives exactly $(-C,A,I\lambda_1-J^\dagger\lambda_2)=\beta(v)$. On a real line the same substitution gives $\alpha=a_z\lambda_1+b_z\lambda_2$ and $\beta=b_z^\dagger\lambda_1-a_z^\dagger\lambda_2$. The scalar-coordinate matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\lambda_1&-\bar\lambda_2\\\lambda_2&\bar\lambda_1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ is invertible whenever $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\ne0$. Solving the two displayed incidence equations similarly recovers a unique $z$ from each point with $\lambda\ne0$; their real-linear coefficient matrix has determinant $(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)^2$. The points with $\lambda=0$ form $L_\infty$. Thus these lines cover $\mathbb P^3$.

At zero real moment, step 1.1 gives $DD^\dagger=\operatorname{diag}(f,f)$ with $f=a^\dagger a=b^\dagger b$. Regularity makes $f$ positive definite by injectivity of $a$, and hence makes $D$ onto. Conversely, surjectivity of $D$ makes both diagonal blocks positive definite; $a$ is injective and $b^\dagger$ onto, so step 2.1 gives regularity. Direct multiplication shows $P^\dagger=P$, $P^2=P$, $DP=0$, and $P$ is the identity on $\ker D$. Inversion of positive matrices is smooth, so [F2] gives the rank-$N$ smooth kernel bundle. Projection of the trivial Hermitian connection is a metric connection because for kernel sections $s,t$, $d\langle s,t\rangle=\langle Pds,t\rangle+\langle s,Pdt\rangle$.

Differentiate $DP=0$ and its adjoint to obtain $dP\,P=-D^\dagger(DD^\dagger)^{-1}dD\,P$ and $P\,dP=-P\,dD^\dagger(DD^\dagger)^{-1}D$. Thus [F3] gives $F=P\,dP\wedge dP\,P=P\,dD^\dagger\operatorname{diag}(f^{-1},f^{-1})\wedge dD\,P$. Its nonzero differential blocks are $dD=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}dz_2&-dz_1\\-d\bar z_1&-d\bar z_2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The resulting two-form blocks are multiples of $dz_1\wedge d\bar z_1-dz_2\wedge d\bar z_2$, $2dz_1\wedge d\bar z_2$ and $2dz_2\wedge d\bar z_1$, with coefficient $f^{-1}$; the $W$ blocks vanish. Expanding in real coordinates shows that these forms are complex linear combinations of $dx^0\wedge dx^1-dx^2\wedge dx^3$, $dx^0\wedge dx^2+dx^1\wedge dx^3$ and $dx^0\wedge dx^3-dx^1\wedge dx^2$. Each has Hodge star minus itself for the positive Euclidean orientation. Multiplication by the degree-zero matrices $P$ preserves this property, so $F^+=0$.

For regular zero-moment data the maps $a_z,b_z$ have orthogonal images and equal positive Gram matrix $f_z$. Therefore $a_z\lambda_1+b_z\lambda_2$ is injective for every nonzero $\lambda$, since its squared norm on $v$ is $(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)\langle v,f_zv\rangle$. The identity with $\sigma$ makes $\beta$ surjective as well. At $L_\infty$, $\alpha=(-\mu_1,-\mu_2,0)^T$ and $\beta=(\mu_2,-\mu_1,0)$ have the same properties. A nonzero maximal minor locally solves each kernel and image equation by holomorphic matrix inversion, so their kernels, images and middle quotient have holomorphic local frames. Hence the middle cohomology is a holomorphic bundle. On a finite real line, split $K=\operatorname{im}a_z\oplus\operatorname{im}b_z\oplus\ker D_z$. Using $a_z,b_z$ to identify the first two summands with $V\oplus V$, and multiplying the target by $f_z^{-1}$, the first two summands form $V$ copies of the Euler complex $\mathcal O(-1)\xrightarrow{(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)}\mathcal O^2\xrightarrow{(-\lambda_2,\lambda_1)}\mathcal O(1)$, whose middle cohomology is zero. The remaining summand is the constant $\ker D_z$, proving the canonical linewise identification. The identical Euler calculation at infinity leaves $W$ with its standard framing.

Under the stated simultaneous torus transformation, $A$ and $C$ acquire factors $t_1,t_2$ and the third component of $\alpha$ acquires $t_1t_2h$. Dividing the resulting middle map by $t_1t_2$ gives $U_K=\operatorname{diag}(t_2^{-1},t_1^{-1},h)$, with source factor $(t_1t_2)^{-1}$ and target factor $1$; direct substitution verifies both chain squares. At infinity the Euler blocks cancel and the induced framing action is precisely $h$. This projective torus action preserves the real-line incidence and commutes with $\sigma$ projectively. In the chart $\lambda_1=1,\lambda_2=0$, the holomorphic coordinates are $(\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)$ with $(\mu_1,\mu_2)=(z_1,z_2)$, so vertical complex orientation followed by the positive stereographic orientation is the complex orientation of $\mathbb P^3$. For $k=0$, $D$ is the unique map to the zero space, $P=1_W$, and all formulas reduce to the framed trivial bundle. No inverse normal-form theorem or global charge calculation was used.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: rank-zero or k=0 spaces use the unique empty matrix and identity projection/frame; no inverse of a positive-dimensional singular matrix is taken.
Statement: k=0 gives the framed trivial bundle in the raw block; the integrable-frame theorem covers the zero operator.
Statement: finite rank one is included by the same matrix/Cauchy proof; raw data allow N=1, while the ASD dictionary remains N>=2.
Statement: moment equations alone do not replace regularity; the block proof proves the rank equivalence, and the local frame proof shrinks to an invertible near-identity gauge.
Statement: the raw block is zero-FI and positive stereographic orientation; it does not identify positive-FI boundary data with ordinary ASD.
Statement: AC is explicit and inherited through exact suppliers; coordinate induction and matrix operations are finite.
Statement: the raw block proves stable/costable imply fiber ranks, and the local frame proof constructs holomorphic charts.
Statement: the raw block proves failure of stability/costability produces a fiber-rank failure; intertwining matrix maps are holomorphic exactly when the local Dolbeault equation holds.

risk_review.notes: Checked all seven steps: b-dagger a is muC; difference of Gram matrices is muR. Common eigenvectors on quotient dual and invariant kernel prove both rank equivalences using muC=0. Zero moments give positive equal Gram blocks, projection and metric connection. Differential two-form blocks are anti-self-dual in the stated orientation. Real-line Euler complexes and infinity ranks give local freeness and triviality; torus chain factors and k=0 are consistent. No inverse or compactification conclusion is smuggled into the forward block.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix an integer $k\ge0$ and $0<\alpha<1$. Write $D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<r\}$ and $\overline D_r:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le r\}$. Let
$$X_{k,\alpha}:=\{q\in C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2;\mathbb C):\operatorname{supp}q\subseteq\overline D_2\},$$
where derivatives are in the real coordinates and the complex-valued Hölder norm is that of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Put $\Gamma(z)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|z|$ and let $Nq=\Gamma*q$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]] and [[def-newtonian-potential]]. Using the Wirtinger derivatives of [[def-wirtinger-derivatives]], define
$$Tq(z):=-4\,\partial_zNq(z),\qquad Sq(z):=\partial_zTq(z)=-4\,\partial_z^2Nq(z).$$

(i) **The Cauchy transform.** For every $q\in X_{k,\alpha}$ and $z\in\mathbb C$,
$$Tq(z)=\frac1\pi\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{z-\zeta}\,dA(\zeta),$$
and this integral is absolutely convergent. The function $Tq$ is smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\overline D_2$, satisfies $\partial_{\bar z}Tq=q$ pointwise, and for every $R>0$ obeys
$$\|Tq\|_{C^{k+1,\alpha}(D_R)}\le C_{k,\alpha,R}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}.$$

(ii) **The derivative.** The function $Sq$ lies in $C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)$ and has the principal-value representation
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\,\operatorname{p.v.}\!\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta),$$
where the principal value uses circular truncations. Equivalently, it is the absolutely convergent subtracted integral
$$Sq(z)=-\frac1\pi\left[\int_{|\zeta-z|<1}\frac{q(\zeta)-q(z)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)+\int_{|\zeta-z|\ge1}\frac{q(\zeta)}{(z-\zeta)^2}\,dA(\zeta)\right].$$
The subtraction is only over the unit disk; no globally absolutely convergent subtraction of $q(z)$ is asserted.

(iii) **Bound on the fixed-support space.** There is $M_{k,\alpha}<\infty$, depending only on $k$ and $\alpha$, such that
$$\|Sq\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)}\le M_{k,\alpha}\,\|q\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\mathbb R^2)},\qquad q\in X_{k,\alpha}.$$
No global $L^p$ mapping property of $S$ is asserted.

Assume AC. Let $P=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\subseteq\mathbb C^n$ be a
polydisc, fix $1\le k\le n$, and let $D_k'\Subset D_k$ be a closed coordinate
disc. There are an open coordinate disc $D_k''$ with
$D_k'\subset D_k''\Subset D_k$ and a cutoff
$\chi\in C_c^\infty(D_k)$ equal to $1$ on $D_k''$ such that the operator

$$T_k g(z)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\mathbb C}\frac{\chi(\zeta)\,g(z_1,\ldots,z_{k-1},\zeta,z_{k+1},\ldots,z_n)}{\zeta-z_k}\,d\zeta\wedge d\bar\zeta$$

is smooth on $P''=D_1\times\cdots\times D_k''\times\cdots\times D_n$ for
every $g\in C^\infty(P)$. On $P''$,
$\partial_{\bar z_k}T_k g=g$. If $\partial_{\bar z_\ell}g=0$ for a selected
set of indices $\ell\ne k$, then
$\partial_{\bar z_\ell}T_k g=0$ for each of them.

For $g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb C^n)$ the same operator without $\chi$ is
globally smooth and satisfies
$\partial_{\bar z_k}T_k g=g$ and
$\partial_{\bar z_\ell}T_k g=T_k(\partial_{\bar z_\ell}g)$ for every
$\ell\ne k$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $k\ge0$ be an integer, $0<\alpha<1$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty. Then $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with the norm of [[def-holder-spaces-c-k-alpha-and-their-scaled-norms]] is a Banach space over $\mathbb K$: every Cauchy sequence in $\|\cdot\|_{C^{k,\alpha}(\Omega)}$ converges in that norm to a limit whose $k$-th partial derivatives are $\alpha$-Hölder on $\Omega$. If in addition $\Omega$ is a bounded $C^{k,\alpha}$ domain with nonempty boundary, then the subspace
$$X_0:=\{u\in C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega): u\text{ extends continuously to }\bar\Omega\text{ with }u|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$$
is closed in $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega)$ and hence is a Banach space. For every bounded open nonempty $\Omega$, the boundary-extension class $C^{k,\alpha}(\bar\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is also a closed subspace of $C^{k,\alpha}_b(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and hence a Banach space, as is its zero-boundary subspace. Completeness here is for the full finite Hölder norm. A boundary Hölder seminorm alone does not define a norm on this function space, since it vanishes on nonzero constant functions.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First solve one equation with all other coordinates regarded as parameters $p$. Write $z_j=\rho w$ on a disk slightly larger than $|w|\le2$, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $|w|<2$ and equal to one for $|w|\le1$, and put $a_\rho(w,p)=\rho A_j(\rho w,p)$. For fixed $0<\alpha<1$, its $C^\alpha_w$ norm is bounded uniformly on a compact parameter polydisc by $C\rho(M_0+\rho M_1)$, where $M_0,M_1$ bound $A_j$ and its first derivatives. Multiplication is bounded in the matrix Hölder norm by the product rule for increments, and [F1] bounds $K(p)u=T(\chi a_\rho u)$ on $C^\alpha(\overline D_2)$. Choose one positive $\rho$ making $\|K(p)\|<1/4$ for every parameter. By [F3], $g=1-K(p)g$ has a unique fixed point; $\|g-1\|\le\|K\|/(1-\|K\|)<1/3$, so $g$ is invertible everywhere. On $|w|<1$, [F1] gives $\partial_{\bar w}g=-a_\rho g$.

The coefficients depend smoothly on parameters as maps into $C^\alpha_w$, since all their parameter derivatives have uniform bounds on compact subsets. The inverse $(1+K(p))^{-1}$ is the uniformly convergent Neumann series; the identity $L(p+h)-L(p)=-L(p+h)(K(p+h)-K(p))L(p)$ for $L=(1+K)^{-1}$ gives its first derivative in operator norm, and induction gives derivatives of every order. Hence $g=L(p)1$ is smoothly parameter-dependent in $C^\alpha_w$. For each such derivative, the fixed-point equation and [F1] gain one $w$ derivative; induction gives all mixed $C^{m,\alpha}_w$ derivatives on the same radius, because only the inverse in the initial $C^\alpha$ space needs smallness. Thus $g$ is jointly smooth. If $A_j$ is holomorphic in an untouched coordinate, $K$ has zero antiholomorphic parameter derivative by [F2], and differentiating the inverse identity gives the same for $g$.

Gauge by this $g$ on the smaller disk. The transformed coefficient is $A_i'=g^{-1}(\partial_{\bar z_i}g+A_i g)$, and $A_j'=0$. The square-zero condition in a smooth frame is $\partial_{\bar z_i}A_j-\partial_{\bar z_j}A_i+[A_i,A_j]=0$, and it is preserved by the gauge transformation by direct conjugation of $(D'')^2$. Therefore every remaining $A_i'$ is holomorphic in $z_j$. Kill the next coordinate by steps 1.1–2.1 with a cutoff only in that coordinate. Their holomorphic-parameter assertion preserves $A_j'=0$. Continue through the finitely many coordinates, shrinking the respective coordinate disks as needed. The product of the resulting smooth invertible gauges has all transformed coefficients zero, proving the required local frame.

If $G$ and $H$ are two such frames, $D''G=D''H=0$ gives $\bar\partial(G^{-1}H)=0$. For smooth scalar functions this implies holomorphy: the one-variable Cauchy formula applies with the other variables fixed, and its iterated integral on a product of small circles gives a locally convergent joint power series. Thus the transition matrices are holomorphic, giving [F4]'s bundle structure; any other structure with the same $D''$ has the same class of holomorphic frames, hence agrees. In these frames an intertwining smooth bundle map has matrix $M$ with $\bar\partial M=0$, so is holomorphic by the same calculation, and the converse follows by the Leibniz rule. Rank zero is immediate and the finite gauge induction covers every positive finite rank.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: rank-zero or k=0 spaces use the unique empty matrix and identity projection/frame; no inverse of a positive-dimensional singular matrix is taken.
Statement: k=0 gives the framed trivial bundle in the raw block; the integrable-frame theorem covers the zero operator.
Statement: finite rank one is included by the same matrix/Cauchy proof; raw data allow N=1, while the ASD dictionary remains N>=2.
Statement: moment equations alone do not replace regularity; the block proof proves the rank equivalence, and the local frame proof shrinks to an invertible near-identity gauge.
Statement: the raw block is zero-FI and positive stereographic orientation; it does not identify positive-FI boundary data with ordinary ASD.
Statement: AC is explicit and inherited through exact suppliers; coordinate induction and matrix operations are finite.
Statement: the raw block proves stable/costable imply fiber ranks, and the local frame proof constructs holomorphic charts.
Statement: the raw block proves failure of stability/costability produces a fiber-rank failure; intertwining matrix maps are holomorphic exactly when the local Dolbeault equation holds.

risk_review.notes: Checked all four proof steps against the fixed-support Cauchy estimate (k>=0, 0<alpha<1), smooth-parameter supplier, Holder completeness and contraction statements. Scaling gives a single uniform operator norm <1/4; cutoff products extend by zero. Operator inverse differentiation and successive Cauchy gains establish mixed smoothness without requiring higher-norm contraction. Integrability preserves killed directions during finite coordinate induction; transition and intertwining matrices satisfy dbar=0. Rank zero is harmless; AC is inherited explicitly. No GAGA premise is used.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $N\geq2$, $k\geq0$, $V=\mathbb C^k$, and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with their standard Hermitian products. A raw datum is $(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$, and $J:V\to W$. Its moment maps are

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

It is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, for $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$, and $w\in W$, span $V$; it is costable if no nonzero common $B_1,B_2$-invariant subspace lies in $\ker J$; it is regular if both conditions hold. Let $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ADHM,reg}}_{k,N}$ be the quotient of the regular zero-moment locus by

$$(B_1,B_2,I,J)\mapsto(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1}),\qquad g\in U(V)$$

The stable complex quotient uses the same formula with $g\in GL(V)$.

Give $S^4=\mathbb H\mathbb P^1$ the unit round metric and positive stereographic orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, where $z_1=x^0+ix^1$, $z_2=x^2+ix^3$. A framed ASD object is a smooth Hermitian rank-$N$ bundle $E\to S^4$ with smooth unitary connection $A$, unitary framing at infinity, $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2=0$, and

$$q_N(E,A)=-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_{S^4}\operatorname{tr}_N(F_A\wedge F_A)=-k,$$

modulo unitary bundle isomorphisms preserving the connection and framing; let $\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}$ be the set of these classes.

Let $T=(S^1)^2\times(S^1)^N$ act on raw data by

$$(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot(B_1,B_2,I,J)=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ),\qquad h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1}),$$

where $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N\in S^1=\{u\in\mathbb C:|u|=1\}$, and on framed ASD classes by inverse pullback under the rotations $(z_1,z_2)\mapsto(t_1z_1,t_2z_2)$ of $S^4$ and postcomposition of the framing by $h$. Assume the following exact conditional supplier conclusions: the zero real quotient is identified diffeomorphically with the stable-and-costable complex $GL(V)$ quotient, and for every $\zeta>0$ the real level quotient with $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ is identified with the stable complex quotient; the stable complex quotient is identified with framed rank-$N$ torsion-free sheaves on $\mathbb P^2$ with a trivialization $\mathcal E|_{L_\infty}\cong W\otimes\mathcal O_{L_\infty}$, with Hilbert polynomial $N\binom{m+2}{2}-k$, and costability is equivalent to local freeness; the framed Ward construction gives a bijection between the specified framed ASD classes and holomorphic rank-$N$ bundles on $Z=\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(\mathbb H^2)=\mathbb C\mathbb P^3$, with $\sigma([v])=[jv]$ for the fixed quaternionic structure $j^2=-1$, that are trivial on every real line, have $c_2=kH^2$ for $H=c_1(\mathcal O_Z(1))$ with $\mathcal O_Z(1)$ the dual tautological line, and carry a nondegenerate holomorphic pairing $b:\mathcal E\otimes\sigma^*\overline{\mathcal E}\to\mathcal O_Z$ satisfying $b_{\sigma z}(v,u)=\overline{b_z(u,v)}$ whose induced form is $h_x(s,t)=b_z(s(z),t(\sigma z))$ and is positive definite on every real-line section space, together with a unitary framing at infinity; and the positive-real linear-monad normal form and its inverse identify each such Ward bundle with a monad $\mathcal O_Z(-1)^{\oplus k}\to\mathcal O_Z^{\oplus(2k+N)}\to\mathcal O_Z(1)^{\oplus k}$ whose zero-moment raw data are regular, modulo $U(V)$. These suppliers retain their stated projective GAGA, family base-change, orientation, charge-normalization, and compact-torus hypotheses.

Under these hypotheses, the construction gives a $T$-equivariant bijection

$$\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ADHM,reg}}_{k,N}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\mathcal M^{\mathrm{ASD}}_{k,N}.$$

For any positive stability level $\zeta>0$, the positive-FI quotient is the quotient by $U(V)$ of $\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$, $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ stable data and can contain non-locally-free framed sheaves; for $N\ge2$ such a point occurs already at $k=1$ by taking $V=\mathbb C$, $B_1=B_2=0$, $J=0$, and any nonzero $I:W\to V$ with $II^\dagger=\zeta$. This boundary is not identified with ordinary framed ASD moduli. The first-order assertion is restricted as follows. Let $D=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ with $\epsilon^\dagger=\epsilon$. The raw modules are free of ranks $k,N$, their moment equations hold over $D$, and their reduction is regular. The monad terms are free of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, its end maps are locally split, its middle cohomology is locally free and commutes with reduction, its global section module is free and commutes with reduction, its coefficient-image submodule is a direct summand and commutes with reduction, and every fixed real-line restriction is trivial with its section module commuting with reduction. The framing and pairing are defined over $D$, positivity is required on the reduction, and allowed base maps are reduction and $\epsilon\mapsto r\epsilon$ for $r\in\mathbb R$. The framed-sheaf family clause additionally requires its three relative cohomology bundles to have ranks $(0,k,0)$, $(0,2k+N,0)$, and $(0,k,0)$ and every stated fiber base-change map to be an isomorphism. Within this range the correspondence is compatible with first-order framed deformations and identifies their tangent spaces.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and equip $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with the standard Hermitian inner products $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$, which are conjugate-linear in the first variable. For a linear map $T:E\to F$ between these spaces, its Hermitian adjoint $T^\dagger:F\to E$ is characterized by $\langle Tu,v\rangle_F=\langle u,T^\dagger v\rangle_E$; in the standard bases its matrix is the conjugate transpose. For $A,B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, define their commutator by $[A,B]:=AB-BA$. Let

$$\mathscr D_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W),\qquad \operatorname{Herm}(V)=\{H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V):H^\dagger=H\}.$$

Here $\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ is regarded as a real vector space. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)\in\mathscr D_{k,N}$. The complex and real moment maps are the maps $\mu_{\mathbb C}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ and $\mu_{\mathbb R}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ defined by

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Assume AC. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$, $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, with their standard Hermitian products. Let $B_i\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, $I:W\to V$, and $J:V\to W$. Define the raw moment maps

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J,$$

and assume $\mu_{\mathbb C}=0$. Put $K=V\oplus V\oplus W$. For $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$ put

$$a_z=(B_1-z_1,B_2-z_2,J)^T,\qquad b_z=(-B_2^\dagger+\bar z_2,B_1^\dagger-\bar z_1,I^\dagger)^T,\qquad D_z=\begin{pmatrix}b_z^\dagger\\a_z^\dagger\end{pmatrix}.$$

Then

$$D_zD_z^\dagger=\begin{pmatrix}b_z^\dagger b_z&\mu_{\mathbb C}\\\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger&a_z^\dagger a_z\end{pmatrix},\qquad b_z^\dagger b_z-a_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb R}.$$

The maps $b_z^\dagger$ are onto for every $z$ exactly when the datum is stable; the maps $a_z$ are injective for every $z$ exactly when it is costable. Consequently, when both moments vanish, regularity is equivalent to $D_z$ being onto for every $z$. On this locus $f_z=a_z^\dagger a_z=b_z^\dagger b_z$ is positive definite and

$$P_z=1-D_z^\dagger\operatorname{diag}(f_z^{-1},f_z^{-1})D_z$$

is the smooth orthogonal projection onto a rank-$N$ bundle over $\mathbb R^4$. The projection connection $\nabla=P\,d$ is unitary and satisfies $F^+=0$ for the positive stereographic orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, where $z_1=x^0+ix^1$, $z_2=x^2+ix^3$.

In homogeneous coordinates $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]$ on $\mathbb P^3$, put $A=B_1\lambda_1-B_2^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_1$, $C=B_2\lambda_1+B_1^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_2$ and

$$\alpha=(A,C,J\lambda_1+I^\dagger\lambda_2)^T,\qquad\beta=(-C,A,I\lambda_1-J^\dagger\lambda_2).$$

The polynomial identity is $\beta\alpha=\lambda_1^2\mu_{\mathbb C}+\lambda_1\lambda_2\mu_{\mathbb R}-\lambda_2^2\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger$. With $\sigma(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$, one has $\beta(v)=\alpha(\sigma v)^\dagger$. The real line over $z$ is $\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2$, $\mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2$; the line at infinity is $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0$. For regular zero-moment data these maps form a holomorphic bundle monad, trivial on each real line, with middle cohomology on the line over $z$ canonically $\ker D_z$. Its framing at infinity is $W$. The torus acts on the homogeneous coordinates by $(\lambda_1,t_1t_2\lambda_2,t_1\mu_1,t_2\mu_2)$ and on the raw data by $(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$; the monad isomorphism has source, middle and target factors $(t_1t_2)^{-1}$, $\operatorname{diag}(t_2^{-1},t_1^{-1},h)$ and $1$, respectively. It preserves the framing representation $W$ with weights $e_\alpha^{-1}$.

This proves a forward raw block construction. It does not assert that every real Ward monad has this normal form, that its inverse extraction is unique, or that the connection extends with charge $k$; those global correspondence and charge assertions require their separate proofs.

Assume full Axiom of Choice. Let $S^4=\mathbb H\mathbb P^1$ have the unit round metric and positive stereographic orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, where $z_1=x^0+ix^1$, $z_2=x^2+ix^3$. Let $E\to S^4$ be a smooth Hermitian rank-$N$ bundle, $N\ge2$, with a smooth unitary connection $A$ and a unitary framing $\Phi:E_\infty\to\mathbb C^N$. Its curvature $F_A$ is an anti-Hermitian endomorphism-valued two-form; set $F_A^+=(F_A+*_gF_A)/2$, where $*_g$ is the Hodge star for the stated metric and orientation, and assume $F_A^+=0$. The determinant-line connection is the connection induced by $A$ on $\det E=\Lambda^N E$. Its framing at $\infty$ determines a unit vector in $(\det E)_\infty$. With

$$q_N(E,A)=-\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_{S^4}\operatorname{tr}_N(F_A\wedge F_A)$$

and determinant Chern-form convention $c(A)=\det(I-F_A/(2\pi i))$, one has

$$q_N(E,A)=-\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle\in-\mathbb Z_{\geq0}.$$

Thus $k=-q_N=\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle$ is a nonnegative integer, with the sign corresponding to the anti-self-dual equation $F_A^+=0$.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

A connection on a finite-rank smooth vector bundle $E\to M$ is flat if and
only if every point of $M$ has a neighborhood carrying a local frame
$(e_1,\ldots,e_r)$ of parallel sections, meaning $\nabla_Xe_a=0$ for every
local vector field $X$ and every $a$.

Let $E\to M$ carry a flat connection, meaning $R^\nabla=0$. For every
$p\in M$ there is a coordinate ball $U$ about $p$ such that, whenever two
piecewise smooth paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to U$ have the same initial
and terminal points,

$$P_{\gamma_0}=P_{\gamma_1}.$$

This is a local assertion; it makes no claim about transport around loops in a
non-simply-connected larger domain.
Assume countable choice. For $n\ge1$, $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(S^n)$ is $\mathbb R$ in degrees $0,n$ and zero otherwise. For $S^0$ it is $\mathbb R^2$ in degree zero and zero otherwise.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, standard Hermitian $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$ and ADHM data $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with the complex equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Stability means that the $B_1,B_2$ words applied to $I(W)$ span $V$; costability means no nonzero common invariant subspace of $V$ lies in $\ker J$; regular means both. Set

$$\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

For every $\zeta>0$, each stable $GL(V)$ orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ in exactly one $U(V)$ orbit, and the inclusion induces a diffeomorphism of smooth real manifolds

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^s/GL(V).$$

At $\zeta=0$, every stable datum satisfying the real equation is automatically costable. Each regular complex orbit meets the zero real level in exactly one unitary orbit, giving instead

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=0,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V).$$

Both identifications are equivariant for the compact rotation/framing torus in the raw-data convention. For $k=0$ all spaces are points. This theorem identifies the stated finite-dimensional quotients; it asserts no correspondence with sheaves or ASD connections, and no identification of the entire positive-FI quotient with the zero-FI regular locus.

derivations.claim: Stabilize a rank-one raw datum by $W'=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, $I'=(I,0)$ and $J'=(J,0)^t$, retaining $V,B_1,B_2$. Then $I'J'=IJ$, $I'I'^\dagger=II^\dagger$ and $J'^\dagger J'=J^\dagger J$. The word span is unchanged and $\ker J'=\ker J$, so both moments and regularity are unchanged. On the finite stereographic chart the raw kernel matrix annihilates the added framing line, and its orthogonal projection is $P_1\oplus1$. Thus [A1] produces a smooth rank-two ASD connection whose restriction to that chart is a line connection plus the flat added line and whose charge is $q_2=-k$. By [F2] its determinant curvature vanishes. On that chart this curvature is exactly the first line's curvature, so the whole rank-two curvature is zero there. Smoothness makes it zero also at infinity, hence $q_2=0$ and $k=0$. Thus no regular rank-one zero-FI datum exists for $k>0$, conditional on the exact retained rank-two input. By [F6], a regular complex rank-one orbit would have such a zero-real-moment representative, so the same emptiness conclusion applies to the complex regular quotient.

Independently, stabilize any framed unitary ASD line connection by the trivial framed flat line. The result is a smooth unitary ASD rank-two connection. Its determinant connection is the original line connection, since $\det(L\oplus\mathbb C)=L$ and the added connection is flat. By [F2] the original connection is flat, so $q_1=0$. Its sector is therefore empty if $k>0$. If $k=0$, transport the unit vector fixed by its framing from infinity. Any two paths differ by a null-homotopic loop by [F3]; subdivide a compact null-homotopy into finitely many cells lying in parallel-frame coordinate balls. Boundary transports in each cell are identity and internal edges cancel, so the loop transport is identity. The resulting global unit parallel section gives the unique framed isomorphism to the trivial flat line. A parallel automorphism fixing its value at infinity is identity. On the raw side at $k=0$ every map is the unique zero-dimensional map, both regularity conditions hold, and $U(0)$ is trivial. This proves the point classification and absence of framed stabilizers.

To type first-order bundle families without presuming a global trivialization, first use step 1.2 to identify the special fiber with its framed parallel line. Choose local lifts of this frame in a locally free Hermitian $D$-line family. If a lift has Hermitian Gram scalar $1+\varepsilon r$ with $r$ real, multiplication by $1-\varepsilon r/2$ makes it unitary, so unitary local lifts exist. Their transition functions have form $1+\varepsilon f_{ij}$, with imaginary-valued smooth $f_{ij}$ and additive cocycle identity. For a subordinate partition $(\rho_k)$, set $u_i=\sum_k\rho_k f_{ki}$ on chart $i$; terms extend by zero where needed. On an overlap, $u_j-u_i=\sum_k\rho_k(f_{kj}-f_{ki})=f_{ij}$. Changing local frames by $1-\varepsilon u_i$ kills the transitions. A constant unitary infinitesimal scalar then matches the given framing at infinity. Hence every such family can be written globally on the fixed framed line as $d+\varepsilon a$, with $a$ a smooth imaginary-valued one-form; the remaining gauge changes are $1+\varepsilon\phi$ with imaginary-valued $\phi$ and $\phi(\infty)=0$.

The coefficientwise ASD equation in this global frame is $(da)^+=0$. Write $a=i\alpha$ for a real one-form. Since $d\alpha$ is ASD, $\int|d\alpha|^2=-\int d\alpha\wedge d\alpha=-\int d(\alpha\wedge d\alpha)=0$ by [F4]. Continuity and nonnegativity imply $d\alpha=0$. Again [F4] gives $\alpha=df$; subtract the constant $f(\infty)$ and put $\phi=-if$. The based gauge $1+\varepsilon\phi$ removes $a$. This gauge is unique: a residual imaginary scalar with zero derivative is constant and its value at infinity is zero. Ordinary framed stabilizers were already trivial in step 1.2. The first-order connection groupoid is therefore the trivial point, not merely a set with one known reduced point.

A regular raw first-order family with $k>0$ would reduce to a prohibited datum from step 1.1, so none exists; the connection family for $k>0$ has no allowable special fiber by step 1.2. At $k=0$ the rank-zero internal $D$-module and all raw maps are uniquely zero, with trivial internal gauge group. Its forward monad is the constant framed line and its forward connection is $d$, also over $D$. Step 3.1 supplies a unique framed gauge from every first-order connection object to this one. Thus this explicit construction is an equivalence of the two first-order groupoids. Reduction and involution-preserving scalar maps commute with it, because the zero datum and the constant line pull back to themselves and the framed trivializing isomorphism is unique. The same argument after complexifying the real tangent spaces gives zero complexified tangent spaces; it does not assert a correspondence for arbitrary complex connections without the Hermitian real condition.

Stabilization intertwines $T$ with the rank-two compact action having framing weights $(h,1)$. In the zero-charge classification, inverse rotations and framing changes send a flat framed object to a flat framed object; the unique framed parallel trivialization identifies it with the same point. Its uniqueness also makes the first-order identifications equivariant. They hold for every first-order Hermitian family defined above, hence also for the subset satisfying the exact locally-free/cohomology-base-change hypotheses retained in [A1]; no extra family statement is obtained from an orbit-set bijection. Positive-FI rank-one stable data and their non-locally-free sheaves and formal fixed-point series were not used in any step.
